docs.title: AeroLog Documentation
docs.text:
AeroLog is a universal, local-first, multi-model storage engine engineered from first principles in pure Rust.

Designed specifically for edge computing, off-grid hardware, wireless P2P mesh synchronization, and mobile platforms, AeroLog replaces traditional page-based B-Tree write amplification with a sequential Append-Only Bitcask Log, hardware-accelerated CRC32 checksums, memory-bounded dual-tier indexing, and monotonic Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC).

docs.title: The Embedded Storage Challenge
docs.text:
Mobile devices, IoT nodes, and off-grid field hardware operate under physical constraints fundamentally different from data center servers: 1. Flash Memory Wear: NAND flash endurance is finite. In-place page overwrites wear out storage cells and trigger costly write amplification. 2. Abrupt Power Cuts: Battery exhaustion, hardware disconnects, and OS process terminations happen without warning. 3. Severe RAM Limits: Mobile operating systems (Android, iOS) aggressively terminate background processes whose memory footprint exceeds platform limits. 4. Lack of Central Coordination: Local-first networks communicate peer-to-peer over intermittent links (Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi Direct, LoRa) without NTP clock servers.

Traditional storage engines were not designed around these four simultaneous constraints.

docs.title: Comparative Storage Paradigms
docs.text:
+-------------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Paradigm          | Primary Data Structure    | Key Limitations on Edge Hardware  |
+-------------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Relational B-Tree | 4KB/16KB Paged Tree       | High write amplification; random  |
| (SQLite, Berkeley)| In-Place Leaf Overwriting | I/O wears flash; page tearing risk|
+-------------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| LSM-Tree          | MemTable + Multi-Level    | Heavy write stalls during merge;  |
| (RocksDB, LevelDB)| SSTable Compactions       | high read amplification (Bloom)   |
+-------------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Append-Only Log   | Bitcask Sequential Log    | RAM bounded by active key count;  |
| (AeroLog)         | In-Memory Dual-Tier Index | requires periodic compaction      |
+-------------------+---------------------------+-----------------------------------+

docs.title: Why Not B-Trees for Edge Sync?
docs.text:
Engines like SQLite use page-based B-Trees. When updating a single 32-byte field in a record, the database engine must: 1. Write the modified 4,096-byte page to a rollback journal or Write-Ahead Log (WAL). 2. Checkpoint and rewrite the 4,096-byte page back to the main database file. 3. Update B-Tree parent navigation pointers if a page split occurs.

This results in a 10x to 100x write amplification factor, generating excessive flash cell erase cycles, wasting battery power, and introducing vulnerability to page tearing during sudden power failure.

docs.title: Why Not LSM-Trees for Off-Grid Nodes?
docs.text: Log-Structured Merge-Trees (such as RocksDB or LevelDB) improve sequential write speed by collecting mutations in a RAM MemTable before flushing them to Level 0 SSTables. However: * Background multi-level compactions generate unpredictably high CPU and I/O spikes. * Point reads often traverse multiple SSTable levels, relying heavily on Bloom filters and large in-memory block caches that exceed mobile RAM allocations.

docs.title: The AeroLog Approach: Bitcask + HLC
docs.text:
AeroLog takes the elegant Bitcask model originally conceived by Eric Brewer and Basho Technologies, and re-engineers it in pure Rust with three critical innovations:

  1. Hardware-Accelerated Integrity: Every single append carries an upfront 32-byte fixed header protected by hardware CRC32. Corrupt tails from unexpected power cuts are isolated instantaneously during cold boot recovery.
  2. Dual-Tier Memory Partitioning: By decoupling mutable Key-Value point entities (indexed in KeyDir) from append-only stream records (indexed in SparseStreamIndex), AeroLog guarantees that message streams (chat, sensors) never flood RAM, maintaining a resident set size strictly under 15 MB.
  3. Native Causality Clocking: Rather than relying on unreliable system wall clocks or NTP daemons, every record header embeds a monotonic Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC). This enables deterministic, zero-conflict Last-Write-Wins (LWW) resolution across distributed peers.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: Understanding when to choose AeroLog—and when an alternative technology is more appropriate—is essential to building robust systems.

docs.title: When to Choose AeroLog
docs.text:
AeroLog is the optimal storage solution when your application satisfies one or more of the following criteria:

  • High-Frequency Writes: You require sustained write throughput exceeding 100,000 writes/second with zero disk write stalls.
  • Flash Memory Longevity: You are deploying on edge appliances, microcontrollers, Raspberry Pi, or mobile devices where flash cell endurance and low power consumption matter.
  • Offline-First & P2P Replication: You are building local-first applications where nodes replicate data peer-to-peer over intermittent wireless links (BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, LoRa) without internet access.
  • Crash-Resilience as a Hard Requirement: You cannot tolerate database corruption caused by unexpected power disconnection, battery loss, or hard reboots.
  • Predictable Low-Latency Point Reads: Your application needs guaranteed \(O(1)\) point reads via direct in-memory coordinate seeks.
  • Strict Memory Budgets: Your application operates within constrained mobile background memory budgets (under 15 MB RSS).

docs.title: When Not to Choose AeroLog
docs.text:
AeroLog is a low-level storage primitive, not an all-purpose relational database management system. You should choose an alternative storage engine (such as SQLite or PostgreSQL) if you require:

  • Complex Relational SQL Queries: AeroLog does not feature a SQL parser, query planner, or declarative query language. If your application relies on JOIN, GROUP BY, or complex nested subqueries, implement them at the application layer or choose a relational engine.
  • Extensive Range Scans on Key-Value Data: KeyDir uses an in-memory hash map. Scanning ordered key ranges (e.g., WHERE key BETWEEN 'order_100' AND 'order_200') requires iterating the map rather than traversing an ordered B-Tree index.
  • Massive Datasets with Tens of Millions of Unique Point Keys on Low-RAM Devices: Because KeyDir keeps an entry in RAM for every unique active key, storing 50 million unique point keys requires several hundred megabytes of RAM. (Note: For large volumes of sequential event logs, use AeroLog Streams, which are sparse-indexed and bounded in memory).
  • Full-Text Search (FTS): AeroLog stores raw byte payloads. Text tokenization, inverted indexing, and phonetic search must be implemented by downstream consumers.

docs.title: Core System Invariants
docs.text:
Every subsystem in AeroLog is designed and validated against four inviolable architectural rules:

  1. Sequential Disk I/O Invariant: The database writer strictly appends to active segment files. In-place modification of existing disk bytes is forbidden.
  2. Dual-Tier Memory Invariant: Stream partitions must never populate the KeyDir. Total RSS memory must remain bounded below 15 MB even when managing 100,000+ stream entries.
  3. Monotonic Causality Invariant: Every written record carries a total ordering tuple (physical_time, logical_counter, node_id_hash) that ratchets forward deterministically upon local writes and remote sync events.
  4. Crash Isolation Invariant: Unwritten, incomplete, or corrupted record fragments resulting from power cuts must be isolated and discarded during recovery without altering valid historical records.

docs.title: What happens if the device loses power during a write?
docs.text: AeroLog writes every record with an upfront 32-byte header containing a hardware CRC32 checksum. If power is interrupted mid-append: 1. The pre-crash records preceding the interrupted write remain fully valid and intact. 2. The trailing partial bytes fail the CRC32 checksum during startup scan. 3. The crash recovery scanner automatically discards the corrupted fragment and truncates the active file segment back to the last known valid record boundary.

docs.title: What is the difference between a Collection and a Stream?
docs.text:
• Collection: Designed for mutable Key-Value entities. Keys in a collection have Last-Write-Wins semantics. Only the latest active value for each key is retained in the KeyDir index. Lookups are \(O(1)\).
  • Stream: Designed for ordered, append-only event logs (e.g., chat messages, sensor logs, audit events). Entries are appended sequentially and are assigned monotonic offsets. Streams use the bounded SparseStreamIndex so that millions of messages do not exhaust RAM.

docs.title: How does AeroLog keep RAM usage below 15 MB for large streams?
docs.text: For point Key-Value collections, every unique key resides in KeyDir. For streams, however, AeroLog applies sparse indexing: it only stores an index checkpoint every \(N\) entries (e.g., entry 0, 100, 200, 300). When seeking entry 254, AeroLog jumps to the checkpoint at 200 and scans forward 54 records sequentially. This bounded index requires only a few kilobytes of RAM per stream partition.

docs.title: Is AeroLog thread-safe?
docs.text: Yes. The AeroLogDb facade is thread-safe and can be safely shared across threads (Arc<AeroLogDb>). Internal write locks protect log segment appends while read operations execute concurrently.

docs.title: Can AeroLog segment files be copied across platforms?
docs.text: Yes. AeroLog uses Little-Endian encoding with explicit byte widths (u16, u32, u64) for all record headers and CBOR payloads. A database directory generated on an Android device (ARM64) can be copied and opened directly on a Linux server (x86-64) or macOS MacBook (Apple Silicon) without data migration.

docs.title: How do I inspect what is stored inside .aerolog files?
docs.text:
Use the built-in CLI diagnostic tool: 

cargo run -p aerolog-cli -- inspect /path/to/data-000000.aerolog
This prints the header fields, CRC32 status, physical timestamps, record types, keys, and payload sizes for every record in the segment.

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text: AeroLog delivers an uncompromising set of storage capabilities engineered for high performance, crash safety, and cross-platform ubiquity.

docs.title: 1. Bitcask Append-Only Storage Engine
docs.text:
• Pure Sequential Appends (\(O(1)\)): Disk writes are appended sequentially to an active .aerolog segment file. No seeking, no block rewriting, and no lock contention on disk pages.
  • Segment Rolling: Active segment files roll over when reaching configurable size thresholds (default: 64 MB), producing sealed immutable historical segments.
  • Single-Seek Random Reads (\(O(1)\)): Point lookups consult the in-memory index and jump directly to the exact file offset and byte length, reading the value in a single I/O operation.

docs.title: 2. Dual-Tier Memory Partitioning
docs.text:
• KeyDir Index: High-speed in-memory hash table mapping (collection, key) pairs to (file_id, offset, length, hlc).
  • Sparse Stream Index: Specialized index for append-only streams (chat messages, telemetry events) that records checkpoints at sparse intervals (e.g., 1 pointer per 100 entries), keeping resident memory footprint strictly bounded under 15 MB.

docs.title: 3. Monotonic Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)
docs.text:
• Physical + Logical Ordering: Formulated around Kulkarni et al.'s HLC algorithm, combining local physical time (epoch milliseconds), an incremental counter for sub-millisecond events, and a deterministic node identifier hash.
  • Distributed Last-Write-Wins (LWW): Provides total causal ordering across nodes without requiring centralized NTP coordination or server consensus.
  • Forward Ratcheting: When receiving records from remote peers during synchronization, the local clock automatically ratchets forward past the highest observed remote timestamp.

docs.title: 4. Hardware-Accelerated Data Integrity & Recovery
docs.text:
• CRC32 Checksum Validation: Every 32-byte record header and variable payload is verified using hardware-accelerated CRC32-IEEE instructions (SSE4.2 on x86-64, ARMv8 CRC32 on aarch64).
  • Defensive Boundary Validation: Slice lengths, string bounds, and buffer boundaries are validated before deserialization to prevent memory corruption.
  • Torn-Write Isolation: Truncated or corrupted trailing record fragments from abrupt system crashes or power failures are automatically identified, logged, and isolated during startup without compromising valid data.

docs.title: 5. Pluggable Compaction & Retention
docs.text:
• Background Log Compactor: Merges sealed historical segments, evicting dead records, overwritten keys, and soft-deleted tombstones into a new compacted segment.
  • Declarative Stream Retention:
  • KeepAll: Retains complete historical stream data.
  • MaxEntries(u64): Caps stream partition size, automatically pruning oldest entries during compaction.
  • TimeToLive(u64): Prunes stream entries older than a specified duration in seconds.

docs.title: 6. Zero-Dependency RFC 8949 CBOR Codec
docs.text:
• Pure Rust Binary Serializer: Standalone aerolog-cbor crate provides binary serialization for structured payloads (maps, arrays, integers, text strings, byte buffers, floating-point numbers).
  • Zero External C/C++ Dependencies: Immune to native memory safety vulnerabilities and buffer overflow exploits.

docs.title: 7. Universal Cross-Platform Bindings (Mozilla UniFFI)
docs.text:
• Multi-Platform Native Support: Full idiomatic bindings for Kotlin (Android and JVM) and Swift (iOS and macOS).
  • Automatic Resource Disposal: Implements Kotlin AutoCloseable and Swift ARC / defer patterns for leak-free memory safety across FFI boundaries.
  • Binary Disk Parity: Storage files created on Android are 100% byte-for-byte compatible with iOS, macOS, Linux, and Windows.

docs.title: Issue tracker: GitHub
docs.text: Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues in untacorp/aerolog. Use the gh CLI for all operations.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Create an issue: gh issue create --title "..." --body "...". Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
  • Read an issue: gh issue view <number> --comments, filtering comments by jq and also fetching labels.
  • List issues: gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]' with appropriate --label and --state filters.
  • Comment on an issue: gh issue comment <number> --body "..."
  • Apply / remove labels: gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..." / --remove-label "..."
  • Close: gh issue close <number> --comment "..."

Infer the repo from git remote -v; gh does this automatically when run inside a clone.

docs.title: Pull requests as a triage surface
docs.text:
PRs as a request surface: no. (Set to yes if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; /triage reads this flag.)

When set to yes, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the gh pr equivalents:

  • Read a PR: gh pr view <number> --comments and gh pr diff <number> for the diff.
  • List external PRs for triage: gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments then keep only authorAssociation of CONTRIBUTOR, FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR, or NONE (drop OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR).
  • Comment / label / close: gh pr comment, gh pr edit --add-label/--remove-label, gh pr close.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare #42 may be either: resolve with gh pr view 42 and fall back to gh issue view 42.

docs.title: When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"
docs.text: Create a GitHub issue in untacorp/aerolog.

docs.title: When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"
docs.text: Run gh issue view <number> --comments.

docs.title: Wayfinding operations
docs.text:
Used by /wayfinder. The map is a single issue with child issues as tickets.

  • Map: a single issue labelled wayfinder:map, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. gh issue create --label wayfinder:map.
  • Child ticket: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (gh api on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put Part of #<map> at the top of the child body. Labels: wayfinder:<type> (research/prototype/grilling/task). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
  • Blocking: GitHub's native issue dependencies, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>, where <blocker-db-id> is the blocker's numeric database id (gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id, not the #number or node_id). GitHub reports issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a Blocked by: #<n>, #<n> line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
  • Frontier query: list the map's open children (gh issue list --state open, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0, or an open issue in the Blocked by line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
  • Claim: gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me, the session's first write.
  • Resolve: gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>", then gh issue close <n>, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to AeroLog will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Bitcask-inspired append-only segment file engine (aerolog-core) with .aerolog files.
  • Monotonic Hybrid Logical Clock (HlcTimestamp) for deterministic causality and total ordering.
  • 32-byte fixed binary record header with per-record hardware CRC32 validation.
  • In-memory KeyDir index with high-concurrency read/write operations.
  • Memory-bounded SparseStreamIndex for append-only streaming workloads (messaging, chat, event logs).
  • Pluggable retention policies (KeepAll, MaxEntries, TimeToLive).
  • Background merge compactor for segment consolidation and tombstone eviction.
  • Zero-dependency compact CBOR codec (aerolog-cbor).
  • Standalone CLI benchmark and diagnostics utility (aerolog-cli).
  • Mozilla UniFFI bindings generator for Kotlin (Android/JVM) and Swift (Apple platforms).

docs.title: Coding & Engineering Standards
docs.text: All contributions to the AeroLog codebase must adhere to the engineering standards detailed below.

docs.title: 1. Zero-Emoji Policy
docs.text: Strictly zero emojis across all code, tests, docstrings, commit messages, PR descriptions, and markdown documentation files.

docs.title: 2. Invariants & Defensive Programming
docs.text:
1. No Panics in Engine Code: Never use unwrap() or expect() in core engine logic. All failure conditions must return an explicit Result<T, AeroLogError>.
  2. Bounds Checking: Always validate slice bounds, length prefixes, and CRC32 checksums before parsing byte buffers to prevent memory corruption.
  3. Hardware Parity: Data generated on one platform must parse byte-for-byte identically on all other supported platforms.

docs.title: 3. Formatting & Linting
docs.text:
Before submitting any code changes, ensure: 

# Code formatting must pass with zero diffs
cargo fmt --all -- --check

# Clippy linter must pass with zero warnings
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings

# All unit and integration tests must pass
cargo test --all

docs.title: 4. Git Commit Messages

docs.title: Reporting a Vulnerability
docs.text:
The AeroLog development team takes security and cryptographic integrity very seriously. If you discover a vulnerability, data corruption hazard, or security flaw:

  1. Do not disclose the issue publicly on GitHub Issues, pull requests, or discussion forums.
  2. Report the vulnerability securely and privately via GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting. This ensures your report is received privately and securely by the maintainers without exposing personal email addresses.

docs.title: ADR 0001: Bitcask Log-Structured Architecture for Mobile Flash Memory
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Traditional mobile databases such as SQLite rely on B-Tree page layouts (typically 4 KB per page). On smartphone NAND flash memory, out-of-order writes and frequent random small mutations incur significant write amplification, leading to premature flash cell wear, elevated battery consumption, and latency spikes during P2P wireless database replication.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We implement a pure append-only Bitcask segment log (.aerolog) architecture: 1. All write operations (put, delete, append) are strictly sequential appends to the active segment file. 2. In-place overwriting of disk bytes is strictly prohibited. 3. Every record is prefixed with a fixed 32-byte binary header containing a 32-bit hardware-accelerated CRC32 checksum. 4. Sealed segment files are merged in the background by LogCompactor to reclaim disk space occupied by overwritten records and soft-deleted tombstones.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) sequential write throughput exceeding 200,000 ops/sec; zero random I/O during writes; battery-friendly; complete immunity to page corruption.
  • Negative: Requires background compaction to reclaim disk space from obsolete records.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Dual-Tier Memory Indexing (KeyDir vs Sparse Stream Index)
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Standard Bitcask implementations store every key in an in-memory hash table (KeyDir). While practical on backend servers with tens of gigabytes of RAM, storing every message key of an active chat system in RAM on low-end mobile devices inevitably triggers operating system Out-Of-Memory (OOM) process termination.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We separate in-memory indexing into two distinct tiers: 1. KeyDir Index: Dedicated exclusively to mutable Key-Value entities. KeyDir maps (collection, key) to disk coordinates (file_id, offset, length, hlc). 2. Sparse Stream Index: Dedicated to append-only streams (chat messages, sensor logs, audit trails). Stream entries are never inserted into the KeyDir. Instead, the engine records sparse checkpoints (e.g., 1 pointer per 100 entries). Sequential range scans read contiguous disk blocks starting from the nearest checkpoint.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Strict memory boundary guaranteed: RAM footprint remains under 15 MB even when holding hundreds of thousands of stream records on disk. Single-seek \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) random reads preserved for Key-Value data.
  • Negative: Stream point reads by arbitrary non-sequential keys are not supported; streams are accessed sequentially or by recent slices.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Native HLC Causality at the Storage Header Layer
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: In partitioned edge and off-grid wireless environments (e.g. disaster relief camps, field logistics), devices have no reliable access to NTP servers. Wall clocks drift and can reset to epoch zero upon battery exhaustion. Storing HLC timestamps as formatted strings (e.g. "1710928300000-0-nodeId") in database columns introduces string allocation overhead and slow lexicographical parsing during replication.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We embed Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC) timestamps directly as native integer fields in the 32-byte binary record header: 

[physical_time: 8B Int64 BE] [logical_counter: 2B UInt16 BE] [node_id_hash: 8B Int64 BE]
Conflict resolution follows total order Last-Write-Wins (LWW): 
\text{HLC}_A > \text{HLC}_B \iff (pt_A > pt_B) \lor (pt_A = pt_B \land lc_A > lc_B) \lor (pt_A = pt_B \land lc_A = lc_B \land node_A > node_B)

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Zero string allocation or parsing overhead during replication scans; deterministic convergence across all distributed replicas; monotonic progression even across physical clock resets.
  • Negative: Last-Write-Wins operates at the record level; fine-grained column-level conflict resolution requires field-level CRDTs.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Pluggable Declarative Stream Retention Policies
Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Mobile edge devices possess finite disk storage. Unbounded append-only streams (such as chat rooms or sensor updates) will eventually exhaust flash capacity if historical entries are never evicted. Hardcoding fixed retention limits directly into the storage engine violates developer flexibility, as medical triage logs require indefinite preservation while temporary telemetry logs only require short-term buffering.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We implement a pluggable, declarative retention contract (RetentionPolicy): - RetentionPolicy::KeepAll: Retains all entries indefinitely (default). - RetentionPolicy::MaxEntries(N): Bounded historical window retaining at most the latest \(N\) entries per stream. - RetentionPolicy::TimeToLive(T): Time-based expiration evicting entries older than \(T\) milliseconds. Retention policies are evaluated and applied during segment compaction cycles by LogCompactor.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive: Product owners and application developers retain full control over disk quotas; obsolete stream entries are reclaimed cleanly without interrupting concurrent operations.
  • Negative: Eviction occurs at compaction boundaries rather than instantaneously upon append.

docs.title: Android & JVM Guide (Kotlin)
docs.text: AeroLog provides high-performance Kotlin bindings generated via Mozilla UniFFI, offering zero-copy buffer handoffs and native coroutines compatibility.

docs.title: 1. Lifecycle & AutoCloseable Management
docs.text:
FfiAeroLogDb implements java.lang.AutoCloseable. Always wrap instances in Kotlin's .use { } block or tie them to an Android ViewModel / Application lifecycle:

import io.aerolog.uniffi.FfiAeroLogDb
import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext
import java.io.File

class StorageRepository(dataDir: File) : AutoCloseable {

    private val db: FfiAeroLogDb = FfiAeroLogDb.open(
        path = dataDir.absolutePath,
        maxSegmentSizeBytes = 64UL * 1024UL * 1024UL
    )

    suspend fun saveUserProfile(userId: String, profileJson: String) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        db.put(
            collection = "profiles",
            key = userId,
            value = profileJson.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
        )
    }

    suspend fun getUserProfile(userId: String): String? = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
        db.get(collection = "profiles", key = userId)?.decodeToString()
    }

    override fun close() {
        db.close()
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Managing Append-Only Streams in Coroutines
docs.text:
Streams are ideal for chat messaging, audit logs, and sensor telemetry:

suspend fun appendChatMessage(roomId: String, messageText: String): ULong = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val stream = db.stream("chat:$roomId")
    stream.append(messageText.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8))
}

suspend fun loadRecentMessages(roomId: String, count: UInt): List<String> = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val stream = db.stream("chat:$roomId")
    stream.readRecent(count).map { entry ->
        entry.payload.decodeToString()
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Distributed Sync & Delta Scanning
docs.text:
Extract incremental mutations for peer-to-peer transmission (e.g. over Bluetooth Low Energy):

suspend fun getDeltaChanges(sinceTimestamp: ULong?): List<Pair<String, ByteArray>> = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val mutations = db.scanMutationsSince(
        sincePhysicalTime = sinceTimestamp,
        sinceLogicalCounter = null,
        sinceNodeHash = null,
        limit = 100u
    )

    mutations.map { record ->
        record.key to (db.get("profiles", record.key) ?: ByteArray(0))
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Triggering Compaction
docs.text:
Reclaim storage space during background maintenance tasks (e.g., Android WorkManager):

suspend fun runMaintenance() = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val stats = db.compact()
    println("Compaction completed: merged ${stats.filesMerged} files, reclaimed ${stats.bytesReclaimed} bytes.")
}

docs.title: The Core Lifecycle
docs.text: Every AeroLog integration follows four steps: 1. Open Database: Provide a storage directory path and configuration. 2. Point Key-Value Operations: Write and read mutable entities by collection and key. 3. Stream Operations: Append ordered events to named stream partitions. 4. Shutdown / Disposal: Close file handles and flush active segments cleanly.

docs.title: Code Walkthrough
Embedded Rust Developer Guide
docs.text: This guide covers building production-grade embedded storage systems using aerolog-core in pure Rust.

docs.title: 1. Engine Configuration
docs.text:
AeroLogConfig allows tuning segment thresholds and retention policies:

use aerolog_core::{AeroLogConfig, AeroLogDb, StreamRetentionPolicy};
use std::time::Duration;

fn initialize_engine() -> aerolog_core::Result<AeroLogDb> {
    let config = AeroLogConfig::new("/var/data/edge_node")
        // Rotate segment files every 64 MB
        .with_max_segment_size(64 * 1024 * 1024)
        // Set sparse checkpoint frequency for streams (1 index entry per 100 records)
        .with_sparse_interval(100)
        // Default retention for streams: keep max 10,000 entries
        .with_default_retention(StreamRetentionPolicy::MaxEntries(10_000));

    AeroLogDb::open(config)
}

docs.title: 2. Point CRUD Operations
docs.text:
AeroLog exposes point Key-Value operations organized by collections:

// Insert / Update (Overwrites existing key via LWW HLC)
db.put("inventory", "item_401", b"{\"name\":\"Widget\",\"qty\":150}")?;

// Point Read
let item = db.get("inventory", "item_401")?;

// Delete (Appends a Tombstone record with monotonic HLC)
db.delete("inventory", "item_401")?;

// Verify Deletion (Returns Ok(None))
assert!(db.get("inventory", "item_401")?.is_none());

docs.title: 3. Append-Only Streams with Retention
docs.text:
Streams are append-only partitions identified by UTF-8 names:

use aerolog_core::StreamRetentionPolicy;

// Open stream with custom retention policy
let chat_stream = db.stream("chat:room_1")?;
chat_stream.set_retention_policy(StreamRetentionPolicy::MaxEntries(5_000));

// Append event
let offset = chat_stream.append(b"Hello edge mesh!")?;

// Read recent entries
let entries = chat_stream.read_recent(50)?;
for entry in entries {
    println!("Offset {}: {} bytes", entry.offset, entry.payload.len());
}

docs.title: 4. Delta Replication Scanning
docs.text:
To replicate local mutations across peers without scanning entire tables, use scan_mutations_since:

use aerolog_core::HlcTimestamp;

// Scan mutations newer than last known remote sync timestamp
let last_sync_hlc = Some(HlcTimestamp::new(1700000000000, 4, 0x12345678));
let new_mutations = db.scan_mutations_since(last_sync_hlc, 500)?;

for mutation in new_mutations {
    println!(
        "Collection: {}, Key: {}, Type: {:?}",
        mutation.collection, mutation.key, mutation.record_type
    );
}

docs.title: 5. Offline & Background Compaction
docs.text:
Reclaim disk space by purging overwritten records and tombstones:

let stats = db.compact()?;
println!("Compacted {} files into 1 segment.", stats.files_merged);
println!("Reclaimed {} bytes of disk space.", stats.bytes_reclaimed);

docs.text: AeroLog provides seamless, memory-safe Swift bindings for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS via Mozilla UniFFI.

docs.title: 1. Opening and Initializing AeroLog in Swift
docs.text:
Initialize the database inside an actor or storage service class:

import AeroLogUniFFI
import Foundation

public actor AeroLogStorageService {
    private let db: FfiAeroLogDb

    public init(directoryURL: URL) throws {
        try FileManager.default.createDirectory(
            at: directoryURL,
            withIntermediateDirectories: true
        )
        self.db = try FfiAeroLogDb.open(
            path: directoryURL.path,
            maxSegmentSizeBytes: 64 * 1024 * 1024 // 64 MB
        )
    }

    deinit {
        db.shutdown()
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Point Key-Value Operations
docs.text:
extension AeroLogStorageService {
    public func save(collection: String, key: String, data: Data) throws {
        try db.put(collection: collection, key: key, value: data)
    }

    public func fetch(collection: String, key: String) throws -> Data? {
        try db.get(collection: collection, key: key)
    }

    public func delete(collection: String, key: String) throws {
        try db.delete(collection: collection, key: key)
    }
}

docs.title: 3. Streaming Event Log
docs.text:
extension AeroLogStorageService {
    public func appendEvent(streamName: String, payload: Data) throws -> UInt64 {
        let stream = try db.stream(streamName: streamName)
        return try stream.append(payload: payload)
    }

    public func fetchRecent(streamName: String, limit: UInt32) throws -> [Data] {
        let stream = try db.stream(streamName: streamName)
        let entries = try stream.readRecent(limit: limit)
        return entries.map { $0.payload }
    }
}

extension AeroLogStorageService {
    public func performCompaction() throws -> FfiCompactionStats {
        return try db.compact()

docs.title: Engine Manual & Internals
docs.text: This section details the inner architecture of AeroLog, explaining how bitcask segments, in-memory indexes, hybrid logical clocks, compactor workers, and cross-platform foreign function bridges cooperate.

docs.text:
1. Bitcask Append-Only Storage: Mechanics of sequential log segments, file rotation, and active vs sealed states.
  2. Dual-Tier In-Memory Indexing: Mathematical structure of KeyDir point lookups and bounded SparseStreamIndex.

docs.title: Memory Ownership & Foreign Lifecycles
docs.text:
Cross-platform FFI bridges are prone to memory leaks and use-after-free bugs if handle lifetimes are not managed strictly. AeroLog enforces clean ownership through:

  1. Foreign Object Handles: Rust engine instances are wrapped in Arc<AeroLogDb> and tracked in a global UniFFI handle table. The host language receives an opaque 64-bit integer pointer.
  2. Deterministic Cleanup in Kotlin: FfiAeroLogDb implements java.lang.AutoCloseable. Calling .close() or exiting a .use { } block notifies Rust to release the internal Arc, freeing native memory immediately.
  3. Deterministic Cleanup in Swift: Swift manages instances using Automatic Reference Counting (ARC). When FfiAeroLogDb goes out of scope, its deinit triggers the UniFFI pointer release callback.

docs.title: Error Handling Across FFI Boundaries
docs.text:
Rust Result<T, AeroLogError> cannot be passed directly as C unions across foreign ABI boundaries. UniFFI maps Rust errors into idiomatic platform exceptions:

  • In Kotlin: Throws AeroLogFfiException (checked or runtime exception).
  • In Swift: Throws Swift errors conforming to Error via throws / try.

docs.title: Hybrid Logical Clocks & Causality
docs.text:
Distributed and off-grid databases cannot rely on physical wall clocks (NTP). Device system clocks drift, can be set backwards by users, and disagree across peers.

AeroLog integrates Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) as a first-class engine primitive, based on the formalization by Kulkarni et al.

docs.title: Structure of an HlcTimestamp
docs.text:
Every record header in AeroLog contains an 18-byte monotonic clock coordinate:

pub struct HlcTimestamp {
    pub physical_time: u64,    // Epoch time in milliseconds
    pub logical_counter: u16,  // Sub-millisecond event sequence
    pub node_id_hash: u64,     // Deterministic peer tie-breaker
}

docs.title: Total Causal Ordering
docs.text:
AeroLog achieves a strict total ordering across all mutations using tuple comparison:

\[ H_1 \lt H_2 \iff \begin{cases} pt_1 \lt pt_2 \\ pt_1 = pt_2 \land lc_1 \lt lc_2 \\ pt_1 = pt_2 \land lc_1 = lc_2 \land node_1 \lt node_2 \end{cases} \]

Where: 1. physical_time tracks the passage of wall-clock time. 2. logical_counter increments when multiple mutations occur within the same physical millisecond. 3. node_id_hash provides a mathematically deterministic tie-breaker if two independent nodes write during the exact same logical counter tick.

docs.title: Forward Clock Ratcheting
docs.text:
When an AeroLog node receives remote changes during peer synchronization:

sequenceDiagram
    participant NodeA as Node A (Local)
    participant NodeB as Node B (Remote)

    NodeB->>NodeA: Send ChangeRecord<br/>(HLC: pt_b, lc_b, node_b)
    Note over NodeA: Update Local HLC:<br/>max(local_pt, remote_pt, wall_clock)<br/>Increment logical counter if equal
    NodeA->>NodeA: Apply ChangeRecord to<br/>Segment & KeyDir
  1. The local clock generator observes (pt_b, lc_b).
  2. The local clock updates its internal state: \(\text{next\_pt} = \max(\text{local\_pt}, \text{remote\_pt}, \text{current\_wall\_clock})\).
  3. This guarantees that any subsequent write produced locally is strictly greater than all previously observed remote events, ensuring causal consistency across wireless mesh networks.

docs.title: Zero-Dependency CBOR Codec
docs.text: The aerolog-cbor crate provides a lightweight, pure-Rust implementation of the RFC 8949 Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) standard.

docs.title: Why CBOR for Embedded Storage?
docs.text:
JSON is human-readable but introduces significant storage and CPU overhead: * Numeric values require decimal string conversion (e.g. 12345678 takes 8 bytes in ASCII vs 4 bytes in binary). * Field names are repeated in every document. * Parsing JSON requires complex string parsing and dynamic memory allocations.

CBOR encodes structured data directly into dense binary representations, reducing payload sizes by 40% to 70% and eliminating parsing CPU overhead.

docs.title: Supported Data Types
docs.text: aerolog-cbor supports full round-trip serialization for: * Unsigned and Signed Integers (0 to 64-bit precision) * Text Strings (UTF-8 encoded) * Byte Strings (Raw binary blobs) * Arrays (Heterogeneous lists) * Maps (Key-value dictionaries) * Booleans and Null

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
use aerolog_cbor::{CborValue, encode, decode};
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Construct structured data
    let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
    map.insert("sensor_id".to_string(), CborValue::Text("temp_01".to_string()));
    map.insert("reading".to_string(), CborValue::Integer(24));
    map.insert("active".to_string(), CborValue::Boolean(true));

    let root = CborValue::Map(map);

    // Encode to binary buffer
    let binary_bytes = encode(&root)?;

    // Decode back from binary buffer
    let decoded_val = decode(&binary_bytes)?;
    assert_eq!(root, decoded_val);

    Ok(())
}

docs.title: Crash Recovery & Data Integrity
docs.text: AeroLog is engineered to withstand abrupt power loss, battery disconnects, kernel panics, and unexpected process termination without database corruption.

docs.title: 1. Hardware-Accelerated CRC32
docs.text: Every record written to disk is prepended with a 32-bit CRC32 checksum computed across both the fixed header fields and the payload bytes. On modern processors, checksum computation uses dedicated CPU vector instructions: * CRC32 instruction via SSE 4.2 on x86-64 * __crc32d instruction via ARMv8-A Cryptography Extensions on aarch64

docs.title: 2. Upfront Length Prefixes
docs.text:
All variable-length fields (key_len, collection_len, val_len) are stored in the fixed 32-byte header. Before reading payloads into buffers, AeroLog validates that:

\[ \text{offset} + 32 + \text{key\_len} + \text{coll\_len} + \text{val\_len} \le \text{file\_size} \]

This prevents buffer over-reads and segmentation faults when encountering malformed or partial writes.

docs.title: The Cold Startup Recovery Scanner
docs.text:
When AeroLogDb::open() executes, the recovery scanner walks all .aerolog files sequentially:

[Record 0: CRC OK] -> [Record 1: CRC OK] -> [Record 2: CRC OK] -> [Torn Bytes: CRC FAIL]
==================================================================>
      Valid Historical State Recovered                             Fragment Discarded
  1. Sequential Traversal: Starts at offset 0 of each file and reads the 32-byte header.
  2. Checksum Verification: Re-computes the CRC32 checksum over the stored header and payload bytes.
  3. If valid: Adds the coordinate to KeyDir or SparseStreamIndex.
  4. If invalid or incomplete:
    • The corrupted trailing fragment is safely discarded.
    • The file is truncated to the end of the last valid record.
    • Recovery completes successfully with zero loss of prior historical data.

docs.title: Bitcask Append-Only Storage
docs.text: AeroLog structures physical data on disk as a sequence of immutable and active log files known as segments.

docs.title: The Log-Structured Model
docs.text:
In traditional in-place update storage systems (like B-Trees), overwriting an existing record modifies bytes in the middle of a file. In contrast, AeroLog enforces an append-only rule: every mutation (insert, update, delete) is appended to the tail of the current active segment file.

data-000000.aerolog (Sealed)   | data-000001.aerolog (Active)
+--------+--------+--------+   | +--------+--------+----------------->
| Rec 0  | Rec 1  | Rec 2  |   | | Rec 3  | Rec 4  | [Next Append]
+--------+--------+--------+   | +--------+--------+----------------->

docs.title: Advantages for Flash & Battery
docs.text:
1. Zero Random Disk Writes: Operating systems and flash controllers stream contiguous blocks sequentially, eliminating internal flash block re-allocation overhead.
  2. Crash Atomicity: Appending bytes to the end of a file guarantees that prior historical records are never partially overwritten if a crash occurs mid-write.
  3. No Lock Contention Between Readers and Writers: Readers seeking historical records in sealed segments never contend with the active segment writer.

docs.title: Segment Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Active Segment: Exactly one segment file is open for both reading and appending (e.g., data-000001.aerolog).
  • Rolling Over: When the active segment file size reaches max_segment_size (configured via AeroLogConfig, defaulting to 64 MB), the writer:
  • Flushes remaining OS buffers to disk.
  • Seals the segment file, making it strictly read-only.
  • Increments the file ID sequence (data-000002.aerolog) and opens the new active segment.
  • Sealed Segments: Immutable files that can be read concurrently by multiple threads without synchronization locks. Sealed segments are eligible for background compaction.

docs.title: Compaction & Retention Policies
docs.text:
Because AeroLog is an append-only engine, updating or deleting records creates dead data on disk. Without compaction, disk usage would grow monotonically.

The Compactor worker and Retention Policy system maintain storage efficiency and prevent disk bloat.

docs.title: The Log Compaction Process
docs.text:
Compaction runs in the background or can be triggered explicitly via db.compact():

flowchart TD
    subgraph SealedFiles ["Sealed Segment Files"]
        S0["data-000000.aerolog<br/>(Dead records & tombstones)"]
        S1["data-000001.aerolog<br/>(Historical mixed records)"]
    end

    subgraph CompactorWorker ["Compactor Engine"]
        CW["Scan Sealed Records<br/>Filter against KeyDir & Retention Rules"]
    end

    subgraph Output ["Compacted Segment File"]
        CS["data-000002.aerolog<br/>(Only active live records)"]
    end

    SealedFiles --> CompactorWorker
    CompactorWorker --> Output
    CompactorWorker -. Delete Reclaimed Segments .-> SealedFiles

docs.title: Compaction Execution Steps
docs.text:
1. The compactor identifies all sealed segment files. (The active segment being written to is left untouched).
  2. For each record in sealed segments:
  3. Key-Value Records: Checks KeyDir. If the record matches the latest in-memory coordinate for that key and is NOT a tombstone, it is written to the new compacted segment. If an older version or tombstone exists, it is discarded.
  4. Stream Records: Evaluates the stream's configured retention policy.
  5. The new compacted segment is sealed and atomically renamed.
  6. KeyDir and SparseStreamIndex update their pointers to point to the new compacted segment file and new offsets.
  7. Obsolete sealed segment files are deleted (unlink), freeing disk blocks immediately.

docs.title: Pluggable Stream Retention Policies
docs.text:
AeroLog supports three declarative retention policies for stream partitions:

pub enum StreamRetentionPolicy {
    KeepAll,
    MaxEntries(u64),
    TimeToLive(u64), // Duration in seconds
}
  • KeepAll: Default policy. All events are retained indefinitely until manually purged.
  • MaxEntries(N): Bounded ring buffer semantics. Compaction only retains the latest \(N\) entries for the stream partition, automatically discarding older entries.
  • TimeToLive(seconds): Expiration semantics. Compaction evaluates each record's physical HLC timestamp against current time, evicting records older than the TTL.

docs.title: Dual-Tier In-Memory Indexing
docs.text:
A fundamental challenge of Bitcask storage engines is in-memory indexing. If every entry in the database requires an in-memory hash pointer, append-only streams (like chat histories or sensor data) will quickly exhaust mobile RAM.

AeroLog solves this through Dual-Tier Memory Partitioning.

docs.title: Tier 1: In-Memory KeyDir (For Key-Value Entities)
docs.text:
The KeyDir is an in-memory hash map that indexes point mutable records:

// Conceptually:
HashMap<(String, String), DiskPointer>
// Where DiskPointer is:
struct DiskPointer {
    file_id: u32,
    offset: u64,
    length: u32,
    hlc: HlcTimestamp,
}

docs.title: Point Read Execution (\(O(1)\))
docs.text:
1. Hash lookup KeyDir.get((collection, key)) retrieves the DiskPointer.
  2. The engine issues a single seek to file_id at offset.
  3. It reads length bytes directly from the segment file into memory.
  4. CRC32 is validated, and the payload is returned to the user.

docs.title: Point Write Execution (\(O(1)\))
docs.text:
1. The record is appended to the active segment file, returning (file_id, offset).
  2. KeyDir.insert() updates the hash table. If the key already existed, the pointer is replaced with the new location and HLC timestamp.
  3. The old record on disk becomes garbage and will be reclaimed during compaction.

docs.title: Tier 2: SparseStreamIndex (For Append-Only Streams)
docs.text:
Stream partitions (chat logs, audit trails, telemetry) append thousands of events over time. If indexed in KeyDir, they would exhaust RAM.

Instead, AeroLog partitions streams into the SparseStreamIndex:

Stream: "sensor_telemetry"
Logical Offset:  0      100     200     300     400
Checkpoints:    [Ptr0]  [Ptr1]  [Ptr2]  [Ptr3]  [Ptr4]  ... (Sparse in RAM)
Disk:           ======================================> (Dense on Disk)

docs.title: Mechanics of Sparse Seeking
docs.text:
• Checkpoint Frequency: An index checkpoint is recorded only once every \(N\) entries (default: 100 entries, configurable via sparse_interval).
  • RAM Footprint: A stream with 100,000 entries requires only 1,000 pointer checkpoints in RAM (~32 KB total memory).
  • Bounded RSS Proof: Even across dozens of active stream partitions and hundreds of thousands of events, total resident set size remains strictly below 15 MB on mobile platforms.
  • Reading an Arbitrary Offset: To read offset 245:
  • Jump directly to the sparse checkpoint at offset 200.
  • Scan forward sequentially 45 records in the segment file.
  • Return the target entry.

docs.title: Binary File Format Specification
docs.text: This document specifies the exact byte-level physical layout of .aerolog segment files. All multi-byte numeric fields are encoded in Big-Endian (Network Byte Order).

docs.title: 2. Fixed Header Byte Layout (32 Bytes)
docs.text: Byte Offset Field Name Data Type Description 0x00 - 0x03 crc32 u32 Hardware CRC32-IEEE checksum of bytes 0x04..0x20 + Body 0x04 - 0x05 magic u16 Magic signature bytes 0x414C (ASCII "AL") 0x06 version u8 Record layout version (currently 0x01) 0x07 record_type u8 0x00 = Put, 0x01 = Delete, 0x02 = StreamEntry 0x08 - 0x0F physical_time u64 Wall-clock epoch millisecond timestamp 0x10 - 0x11 logical_counter u16 Monotonic sub-millisecond logical counter 0x12 - 0x19 node_id_hash u64 FNV-1a 64-bit hash of originating node identifier 0x1A - 0x1B key_len u16 Length of the composite key string in bytes 0x1C - 0x1F value_len u32 Length of the Payload/Value in bytes

docs.title: 3. Record Body Layout
docs.text:
Immediately following byte 0x1F of the header:

Field Name Length in Bytes Description key key_len UTF-8 String (collection:key for KV; stream_id for streams) value value_len Raw Binary Payload (CBOR, JSON, binary blob)

Total record length on disk:

\[ \text{Total Bytes} = 32 + \text{key\_len} + \text{value\_len} \]

docs.title: 4. Checksum Calculation Scope
docs.text:
The crc32 field at bytes 0x00..0x03 protects all subsequent bytes of the record:

\[ \text{CRC32}(\text{bytes}[0x04 \dots 0x1F] \,\|\, \text{body\_bytes}) \]

During read operations, the engine calculates the checksum over this slice and asserts equality with crc32.

docs.title: CLI Command Reference (aerolog)
docs.text: Complete flag, command, and REPL reference for the aerolog-cli binary.

docs.title: Global Options
docs.text:
aerolog [--db <PATH>] [COMMAND]
  • --db, -d <PATH>: Filesystem path to the AeroLog database directory (default: ./aerolog_data).
  • --help, -h: Prints command help and exits.
  • --version, -V: Prints current version.

Running aerolog without arguments launches the Interactive Database Shell (REPL).

docs.title: 1. put
docs.text:
Stores a Key-Value pair in a specified collection, generating a monotonic HLC timestamp.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] put <COLLECTION> <KEY> <VALUE>

aerolog --db ./storage put users alice '{"name":"Alice","role":"admin"}'

docs.title: 2. get
docs.text:
Retrieves a record payload by collection and key via single-seek KeyDir lookup.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] get <COLLECTION> <KEY>

aerolog --db ./storage get users alice

docs.title: 3. delete
docs.text:
Soft-deletes a record by appending an immutable tombstone record.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] delete <COLLECTION> <KEY>

aerolog --db ./storage delete users alice

docs.title: 4. scan
docs.text:
Scans and displays all live, non-deleted key-value pairs in a collection.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] scan <COLLECTION>

aerolog --db ./storage scan users

docs.title: 5. stream
docs.text: Manages append-only event streams (chat partitions, sensor metrics, changelogs).

docs.title: Stream Actions
docs.text:
• append <STREAM_ID> <PAYLOAD>: Appends an event to the stream partition.
  • read <STREAM_ID> [--limit <N>]: Reads the most recent \(N\) events from the stream (default limit: 10).
  • info <STREAM_ID>: Displays total entry count for the stream partition.
# Append an event
aerolog stream append mesh_chat "Node B joined cluster"

# Read recent 20 messages
aerolog stream read mesh_chat --limit 20

# View stream metadata
aerolog stream info mesh_chat

docs.title: 6. compact
docs.text:
Triggers offline segment compaction, merging sealed .aerolog files, evicting dead records and expired tombstones, and applying retention policies.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] compact

docs.title: 7. inspect
docs.text:
Displays physical segment counts, active segment identifier, and disk usage metrics.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] inspect

docs.title: 8. dump
docs.text:
Sequentially scans and dumps all decoded physical records from disk to stdout.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] dump

docs.title: 9. repl (Interactive Database Shell)
docs.text:
Launches an interactive prompt to execute database operations continuously without re-opening files on every command.

aerolog [--db <PATH>] repl
